passage:
Dear Yogesh bhaiya,
Remember I said the science project would take one evening? It took four, and I started last night. I was up till three gluing the model, and I only finished because the deadline was screaming at me. Mummy found me asleep on the chart paper.
I honestly thought I had loads of time. Every week it's like this. Time just disappears on me, and then suddenly it's tomorrow.
Papa gave me the usual lecture about discipline. I know all that. It doesn't help. What helped last term was when you sat with me and broke the history essay into five small parts with dates on the calendar.
Could we do that for the maths assignment? Maybe a timer too, and a reminder on my phone every Sunday.
Thanks,
Vishal

qa.q: Until what time was Vishal up gluing the model?
qa.a: Till three.

qa.q: How does Vishal feel about always rushing at the last minute?
qa.a: Vishal feels frustrated and helpless, saying time just disappears and that lectures about discipline don't help.

qa.q: What help does Vishal ask for, and why might it work better than a lecture?
qa.a: Breaking the maths assignment into small dated parts, plus a timer and Sunday reminders, gives outside structure that lectures don't.

qa.q: How might Yogesh bhaiya feel reading that the help last term worked?
qa.a: Yogesh bhaiya might feel glad and trusted, and ready to sit down with Vishal again.

grounding: Shows a teenager who underestimates how long tasks take and works only under deadline pressure, and who finds outside structure more useful than lectures.

passage:
Rafiq, you won't believe this. The history project was given three weeks ago, right? I kept thinking, it's fine, I'm quick. Then last night at nine, Ammi asked, 'Wasim, isn't that due tomorrow?' and my stomach just dropped.
I did the whole thing in one night. Honestly, some of it's good, because when the deadline is right there my brain finally switches on. But I was shaking by morning and forgot my lunch.
Ammi didn't shout. She said, 'Lectures haven't worked, so let's try something else.' She's put a big wall calendar in the kitchen. Every project gets split into mini-deadlines, in different colours. And on Sunday nights she sits with me for ten minutes to look at the week.
It feels babyish. But the geography chart is already half done. That's never happened.

qa.q: When was the history project given?
qa.a: Three weeks ago.

qa.q: What did Wasim feel when Ammi asked about the due date?
qa.a: Wasim felt a sudden drop of panic on realising the project was due tomorrow.

qa.q: What choice did Ammi make instead of shouting?
qa.a: She put up a big wall calendar with colourful mini-deadlines and sits with Wasim for ten minutes on Sunday nights to look at the week.

qa.q: How might Ammi feel seeing the geography chart half done early?
qa.a: Ammi may feel relieved and hopeful that outside structure is working better than lectures did.

grounding: Shows a teenager who starts late and works only under deadline pressure, and a parent who replaces lectures with outside structure.

passage: Kavitha, you think the project will take one evening? I used to think like that. At fifteen, in Pune, I'd start the science model the night before it was due, sure it would take an hour. It took six, every time. I'd be gluing at three in the morning, my mother shaking her head. And close to the deadline I worked brilliantly; that was the strange part. But before that, nothing. My teacher, Mrs Kulkarni, didn't lecture. She broke my next project into five small pieces with five dates and asked to see one piece each Friday. I, Chinmay, grumbled. But for the first time I slept the night before. Structure helped me more than any scolding.

qa.q: How many pieces did Mrs Kulkarni break the project into?
qa.a: Five small pieces.

qa.q: How did young Chinmay feel about the new plan at first?
qa.a: Chinmay felt grumpy and resistant, grumbling about it.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: Mrs Kulkarni's five dated pieces with Friday check-ins gave outside structure instead of a lecture.

qa.q: How might Chinmay's mother have felt at three in the morning?
qa.a: She probably felt frustrated and worried, shaking her head at the late-night rush.

grounding: Shows a teen who underestimated how long tasks took and rushed at the deadline, helped by outside structure rather than lectures.

passage: The college-application essay was due at midnight, and at nine Anand still thought he had plenty of time. "It's only five hundred words," he told his sister, Bidisha. Then the internet dropped in their building. He paced, switched to his phone's data, and realised he hadn't even started the second question. By eleven he was sweating, typing faster than he ever had, and the writing was good, as it always was under pressure. He submitted at 11:56. Bidisha watched him collapse on the bed. "Every time, Anand." "I know," he groaned. "I really thought it'd take an hour." She pulled out her phone. "Next deadline, I'm putting three reminders in your calendar and checking in with you. No lectures." He nodded, grateful.

qa.q: When did Anand submit the essay?
How was Anand feeling by eleven?
qa.a: He was stressed and sweating, rushing to finish.

qa.q: How does Bidisha plan to help, and why might it work?
qa.a: Three calendar reminders and check-ins with no lectures, giving outside structure for a real planning difficulty.

qa.q: How does Bidisha feel watching the last-minute rush?
qa.a: Bidisha seems exasperated but caring, choosing to help rather than scold.

grounding: Illustrates a teen who underestimates time, starts late and works only under pressure, helped by outside structure.

passage: Pradeep had meant to start revising for the history test on Monday. Then on Tuesday. On Thursday night, with the test the next morning, he opened his book at ten and discovered there were six chapters, not two. In their Dadar flat, his mother, Swati, found him at midnight, surrounded by notes, pale and panicking. She wanted to say, "Why do you always do this?" She had said it a hundred times; it never helped. So instead, on Saturday, she put a whiteboard by his desk, and together they broke the next test into small daily chunks, each with a time. "I'll check with you at eight every evening," she said. "Just a tick." For the next test, Pradeep finished revising a full day early. He didn't quite believe it.

qa.q: How many chapters did Pradeep discover there were?
qa.a: Six chapters, not two.

qa.q: How was Pradeep feeling at midnight?
qa.a: He was pale and panicking, overwhelmed by the work left.

qa.q: Why did Swati's whiteboard plan work better than her usual question?
qa.a: It gave Pradeep outside structure with small daily chunks and a check-in, instead of a lecture that never helped.

qa.q: How might Swati feel when Pradeep finishes a day early?
qa.a: Swati likely feels relieved and proud that the new approach worked.

grounding: Shows a teen whose time blindness leads to last-minute panic, helped by a parent's structure instead of lectures.

passage:
"Lalit, the science model is due tomorrow," Kashish said from the doorway. "You said you'd start on Saturday."
"I did start. I bought the thermocol."
"It's Wednesday night."
"It'll take one hour, Didi. Two max."
"That's what you said about the history chart. It took five."
Lalit rubbed his face. "I don't know why it always goes like this. I really thought I had time."
"I'm not going to lecture you. Let's just split it. What are the steps?"
"Cut the base. Paint. Wires. Labels."
"Okay. Timer for each. Base, twenty minutes. Go."
The alarm rang. Lalit looked up, shocked. "The base alone took twenty?"
"Now you know. Next project, we write the steps on the calendar the day it's set."
"Deal. Can you time the paint too?"

qa.q: What did Lalit buy on Saturday?
qa.a: He bought the thermocol.

qa.q: How did Lalit feel when he said he didn't know why it always goes like this?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and confused with himself, because he genuinely believed he had enough time.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what did Kashish do that could fix it?
qa.a: Lalit underestimated how long tasks take; Kashish broke the job into steps with timers and planned to put future steps on a calendar, giving him outside structure.

qa.q: If Kashish had lectured instead, what might change?
qa.a: Lalit might feel ashamed and defensive, and he still wouldn't learn how long each step actually takes.

grounding: Lalit underestimates how long his project will take and starts late, and his sister gives outside structure instead of a lecture.
